words.meaning: provide room or make adjustments for

Safety is a major concern.

grammars.title: Modals use a bare infinitive
grammars.rule: After can, could, may, might, must, should or would, use the base verb without to.
grammars.correct: She should contact the office.
grammars.incorrect: She should to contact the office.
grammars.explanation: Modals are followed directly by the base verb.

grammars.title: Must versus have to
grammars.rule: Must expresses strong obligation or deduction; have to often signals external necessity. Must not means prohibition; don't have to means no obligation.
grammars.correct: You don't have to attend the optional seminar.
grammars.incorrect: You must not attend the optional seminar to mean optional.
grammars.explanation: Must not prohibits; don't have to means optional.

grammars.title: Polite requests
grammars.rule: Use could you / would you and would you mind + -ing to sound courteous.
grammars.correct: Would you mind opening the window?
grammars.incorrect: Would you mind to open the window?
grammars.explanation: The common would you mind request pattern takes an -ing verb.

grammars.title: May / might / must certainty
grammars.rule: May and might signal possibility; must can express a strong inference rather than a rule.
grammars.correct: The door is locked; the office must be closed.
grammars.incorrect: The door is locked; the office must closing.
grammars.explanation: A deduction uses must + base verb.

grammars.title: Advice and consequences
grammars.rule: Should commonly gives advice, whereas would often describes a hypothetical preference or result.
grammars.correct: You should read the instructions first.
grammars.incorrect: You would read the instructions first as ordinary direct advice.
grammars.explanation: Should is the natural modal for direct advice.

traps.incorrect: You must to register today.
traps.correct: You must register today.
traps.explanation: Must is followed by a base verb.

traps.incorrect: You don't must attend.
traps.correct: You don't have to attend.
traps.explanation: For absence of obligation use don't have to.

traps.incorrect: Would you mind to help me?
traps.correct: Would you mind helping me?
traps.explanation: Would you mind is followed by -ing.

traps.incorrect: May you explain it to me?
traps.correct: Could you explain it to me?
traps.explanation: Could you is the natural request pattern.

traps.incorrect: I am interesting in the course.
traps.correct: I am interested in the course.
traps.explanation: Interested describes the person's feeling.

traps.incorrect: I look forward to hear from you.
traps.correct: I look forward to hearing from you.
traps.explanation: To is a preposition here, followed by -ing.

traps.incorrect: Please inform to me the details.
traps.correct: Please inform me of the details.
traps.explanation: Inform someone of/about something.

traps.incorrect: I need an extension until next Friday please.
traps.correct: I would appreciate an extension until next Friday.
traps.explanation: Courteous requests are especially valuable in TOEFL email tasks.

parts.title: Gerunds and Infinitives
parts.focus: Verb complementation, purposes and learning strategies

words.example: Students acquire skills through practice.
It takes time to master pronunciation.
She practices speaking every day.
The student revised the essay.
Spaced review helps retain vocabulary.
Try to recall the word before revealing it.

words.meaning: learn so that something can be recalled
words.example: He memorized the main definitions.
Readers must comprehend the author's argument.
It is hard to concentrate in a noisy room.
The lesson focuses on sentence structure.
Students engage in group discussion.
Everyone participated in the debate.
Two departments collaborated on the project.
The students cooperated on the assignment.
Researchers attempted to reproduce the result.

words.meaning: plan or mean to do something
words.example: The committee intends to publish the report.
The workshop aims to improve communication.

words.meaning: work very hard toward a goal
words.example: Learners strive to become more fluent.
I prefer reading articles to watching videos.
Many students enjoy learning languages.
Avoid repeating the same argument.
The team considered changing the timetable.
The mentor suggested joining a study group.
The professor recommended reading the chapter.
They postponed holding the seminar.
The authors admitted making a mistake.

words.meaning: state that something is not true
words.example: The manager denied receiving the complaint.
The participant refused to answer.

words.meaning: accept a proposal or share an opinion
words.example: They agreed to revise the schedule.
The committee decided to continue.
Students expect to receive feedback.
She managed to finish the task.
The experiment failed to confirm the hypothesis.
The teacher encouraged students to speak.
The library allows students to borrow tablets.

phrases.example: I look forward to meeting you.

phrases.meaning: want to do or learn something
phrases.example: She is interested in studying linguistics.
The system is capable of processing audio.
He has difficulty understanding accents.
Students spend time reviewing notes.
Avoid copying whole sentences.
They decided to extend the deadline.

The office agreed to help.
We plan to study abroad.
Consider taking detailed notes.
She is used to speaking in public.
He used to study late.
We meet weekly in order to share progress.

grammars.title: Verbs followed by -ing
grammars.rule: Enjoy, avoid, finish and consider normally take gerunds as verb complements.
grammars.correct: She enjoys studying biology.
grammars.incorrect: She enjoys to study biology.
grammars.explanation: Enjoy normally takes a gerund.

grammars.title: Verbs followed by to-infinitive
grammars.rule: Decide, hope, plan, promise and refuse generally take to + base verb.
grammars.correct: They decided to postpone the exam.
grammars.incorrect: They decided postponing the exam.
grammars.explanation: Decide is normally followed by to-infinitive.

grammars.title: Prepositions + gerund
grammars.rule: A verb after a preposition is generally expressed as an -ing form.
grammars.correct: She is interested in learning English.
grammars.incorrect: She is interested in learn English.
grammars.explanation: In is a preposition, so use the gerund.

grammars.title: Stop doing versus stop to do
grammars.rule: Stop doing means end the activity; stop to do means pause another activity for a purpose.
grammars.correct: She stopped studying to answer the phone.
grammars.incorrect: She stopped to studying to answer the phone.
grammars.explanation: Stop to + base verb expresses purpose.

grammars.title: Suggest + gerund
grammars.rule: Suggest commonly takes a noun, gerund or that-clause, not a personal object + to-infinitive.
grammars.correct: The professor suggested reviewing the outline.
grammars.incorrect: The professor suggested us to review the outline.
grammars.explanation: Use suggested that we review or suggested reviewing.

traps.incorrect: She enjoys to read.
traps.correct: She enjoys reading.
traps.explanation: Enjoy normally takes a gerund.

traps.incorrect: We decided going early.
traps.correct: We decided to go early.
traps.explanation: Decide takes a to-infinitive.

traps.incorrect: I look forward to meet you.
traps.correct: I look forward to meeting you.
traps.explanation: Look forward to uses preposition to plus -ing.

traps.incorrect: They avoided to answer.
traps.correct: They avoided answering.
traps.explanation: Avoid takes a gerund.

traps.incorrect: He suggested me to leave.
traps.correct: He suggested that I leave.
traps.explanation: Suggest does not normally take object + to-infinitive.

traps.incorrect: She made me to repeat.
traps.correct: She made me repeat.
traps.explanation: Active causative make takes the bare infinitive.

traps.incorrect: I am used to wake up early.
traps.correct: I am used to waking up early.
traps.explanation: Be used to takes a noun or gerund.

traps.incorrect: I stopped to smoke last year meaning I quit.
traps.correct: I stopped smoking last year.
traps.explanation: Stopping an ongoing habit takes stop + -ing.

words.example: Heat can transform liquid water into vapor.

words.example: The company manufactures medical devices.

words.meaning: send from one place to another
words.example: Signals are transmitted through cables.

words.meaning: remove or obtain from a material
words.example: Scientists extract DNA from the sample.
The team isolated a single variable.
The technique combines two methods.
The course integrates listening and speaking.
The researchers modified the original design.
Animals adapt to new environments.
The technician adjusted the instrument.
The government regulates water quality.
The museum preserves ancient artifacts.
Efficient devices conserve energy.
Volunteers restored the wetland.
LED lamps replace older bulbs.
The filter eliminates most impurities.
Sensors detect changes in pressure.
The device measures oxygen levels.
The system calculates the average.
The thermometer records the temperature.
Researchers observed animal behavior.
Technicians inspect the bridge each year.
The device operates automatically.
The membrane functions as a barrier.
The chemicals react when mixed.

words.meaning: allow to escape or make public
words.example: The reaction releases heat.
Dark surfaces absorb more sunlight.
Cars emit exhaust gases.

phrases.example: The device is composed of three layers.
The container is made of glass.

grammars.title: Passive formation
grammars.rule: Use an appropriate form of be plus the past participle.
grammars.correct: The equipment was installed yesterday.
grammars.incorrect: The equipment was install yesterday.
grammars.explanation: Installed is the required past participle.

grammars.title: Tense preservation
grammars.rule: When switching from active to passive, preserve the event's tense.
grammars.correct: They have completed the work. → The work has been completed.
grammars.incorrect: They have completed the work. → The work was completed when preserving the exact tense.
grammars.explanation: Present perfect passive uses has/have been + participle.

grammars.title: Agent with by
grammars.rule: Use by to introduce the agent when it matters.
grammars.correct: The procedure was developed by engineers.
grammars.incorrect: The procedure was developed from engineers.
grammars.explanation: From marks origin/source, not the agent in this case.

grammars.title: Passive with modals
grammars.rule: Use modal + be + past participle.
grammars.correct: The samples must be stored safely.
grammars.incorrect: The samples must stored safely.
grammars.explanation: Passive after a modal requires be.

grammars.title: Not every verb passivizes
grammars.rule: An intransitive verb such as arrive has no direct object to move into passive subject position.
grammars.correct: The train arrived late.
grammars.incorrect: The train was arrived late.
grammars.explanation: Arrive is intransitive; the given passive is not valid.

traps.incorrect: The experiment has conducted yesterday.
traps.correct: The experiment was conducted yesterday.
traps.explanation: Past finished event needs was + participle.

traps.incorrect: The samples must stored safely.
traps.correct: The samples must be stored safely.
traps.explanation: Passive with modal needs be.

traps.incorrect: The report was wrote by a student.
traps.correct: The report was written by a student.
traps.explanation: Past participle of write is written.

traps.incorrect: The train was arrived late.
traps.correct: The train arrived late.
traps.explanation: Arrive is intransitive.

traps.incorrect: The device consists from three parts.
traps.correct: The device consists of three parts.
traps.explanation: Consist takes of.

traps.incorrect: The experiment was happened last night.
traps.correct: The experiment happened last night.
traps.explanation: Happen has no ordinary passive form.

traps.incorrect: The data have been collect.
traps.correct: The data have been collected.
traps.explanation: Present perfect passive needs been + participle.

traps.incorrect: The results were obtained by the river.
traps.correct: The results were obtained from the river.
traps.explanation: From is natural for the source of samples or data.

parts.title: Conditionals and Cause
parts.focus: Hypothetical situations, consequences and cautious predictions

words.example: One consequence of drought is crop failure.
The new policy had a positive impact.

Economists forecast moderate growth.
The probability of rainfall is low.
The likelihood of error decreases with training.
Exposure increases the risk of illness.
Flooding poses a hazard to residents.
Coastal areas are vulnerable to flooding.
Resilient ecosystems recover after disturbances.
Young plants are susceptible to frost.
Some degree of wear is inevitable.
The final outcome remains uncertain.
Several explanations are possible.
The approach offers potential benefits.
The plan is feasible within the budget.
The council proposed an alternative route.

words.meaning: possible set of conditions or events
words.example: The team explored a worst-case scenario.
The model relies on one major assumption.
Light intensity was the independent variable.
Time was the primary constraint.
The device activates above a threshold.
Plants grow well under suitable conditions.
Under these circumstances, delay is sensible.

words.meaning: be more important or greater than
words.example: The benefits outweigh the costs.
Lower fuel use may offset some expenses.
Vaccination can prevent some infections.
Regular maintenance helps avoid breakdowns.
The new system reduces energy use.
Rainfall may increase in winter.

phrases.example: We can extend the trial if necessary.
In the event of a fire, use the stairs.

phrases.meaning: only if a condition is met
phrases.example: The program will proceed provided that funding continues.

phrases.meaning: except when a different rule is given
phrases.example: All fees are final unless otherwise stated.
Under these circumstances, the plan should change.
Prices are likely to rise.
The system is unlikely to fail.
The crop failed as a result of drought.
Poor drainage can lead to flooding.
The update resulted in fewer errors.
The conflict stems from a misunderstanding.
The experiment gave rise to further questions.
Pollution poses a risk to wildlife.
Success depends on consistent practice.
Admission is conditional on meeting the requirements.

grammars.title: Zero conditional
grammars.rule: Use if + present, present for general truths.
grammars.correct: If water freezes, it expands.
grammars.incorrect: If water will freeze, it expands.
grammars.explanation: A general scientific condition ordinarily uses present simple.

grammars.title: First conditional
grammars.rule: Use if + present, will/may/can + base verb for realistic future possibilities.
grammars.correct: If it rains, we will stay indoors.
grammars.incorrect: If it will rain, we will stay indoors.
grammars.explanation: Future condition uses present form.

grammars.title: Second conditional
grammars.rule: Use if + past, would + base for unreal/hypothetical present or future.
grammars.correct: If I had more time, I would practice daily.
grammars.incorrect: If I would have more time, I practiced daily.
grammars.explanation: The hypothetical if-clause uses past form, not would.

grammars.title: Third conditional
grammars.rule: Use if + past perfect, would have + past participle for unreal past alternatives.
grammars.correct: If they had tested it, they would have found the error.
grammars.incorrect: If they would test it, they would have found the error.
grammars.explanation: Unreal past condition uses had + past participle.

grammars.title: Unless is if not
grammars.rule: Unless introduces an exception/negative condition; do not add not if it reverses the intended meaning.
grammars.correct: Unless the temperature falls, the ice will melt.
grammars.incorrect: Unless the temperature does not fall, the ice will melt to mean the same thing.
grammars.explanation: Adding not reverses the condition.

traps.incorrect: If I will have time, I will call.
traps.correct: If I have time, I will call.
traps.explanation: First conditional if-clause uses present.

traps.incorrect: If I would know, I would tell you.
traps.correct: If I knew, I would tell you.
traps.explanation: Second conditional uses past in if-clause.

traps.incorrect: If she studied, she would have passed yesterday.
traps.correct: If she had studied, she would have passed yesterday.
traps.explanation: Unreal past requires past perfect.

traps.incorrect: Unless you don't revise, you will forget meaning if no revision.
traps.correct: Unless you revise, you will forget.
traps.explanation: Unless already means if not.

traps.incorrect: This policy may causes problems.
traps.correct: This policy may cause problems.
traps.explanation: Modal takes bare infinitive.

traps.incorrect: The results depend of temperature.
traps.correct: The results depend on temperature.
traps.explanation: Fixed phrase depends on.

traps.incorrect: This may lead into damage.
traps.correct: This may lead to damage.
traps.explanation: Cause/result collocation is lead to.

traps.incorrect: The benefit outweigh the cost.
traps.correct: The benefits outweigh the costs.
traps.explanation: Plural subject benefits uses base verb.

words.example: The speaker referred to an earlier study.

words.meaning: short and clear without unnecessary words
words.example: A concise answer is easier to follow.

grammars.title: Defining relative clauses
grammars.rule: Use who for people and which/that for things to identify exactly which person or thing is meant.
grammars.correct: The student who won the award studies biology.
grammars.incorrect: The student which won the award studies biology.
grammars.explanation: Who identifies people.

grammars.title: Non-defining clauses
grammars.rule: Use commas for extra information; use who or which, not that, in conventional non-defining clauses.
grammars.correct: The lecture, which began at nine, was useful.
grammars.incorrect: The lecture, that began at nine, was useful.
grammars.explanation: Non-defining clauses are set off by commas and use which/who.

grammars.title: Possessive relative whose
grammars.rule: Use whose for possession or association, including inanimate nouns.
grammars.correct: The researcher whose article we read is visiting.
grammars.incorrect: The researcher which article we read is visiting.
grammars.explanation: Whose acts as a possessive relative determiner.

grammars.title: Reduced relative clauses
grammars.rule: A relative clause using be + participle can sometimes be reduced by deleting relative pronoun and be.
grammars.correct: The data collected yesterday were verified.
grammars.incorrect: The data that collected yesterday were verified.
grammars.explanation: The data are the receiver of collecting, so use passive participle or that were collected.

grammars.title: Pronoun reference clarity
grammars.rule: Make sure it/they/this points unambiguously to the intended noun or event.
grammars.correct: The experiment failed; this failure prompted a redesign.
grammars.incorrect: The experiment failed because it was expensive, when it has no clear referent.
grammars.explanation: Explicit repetition can remove ambiguous pronoun references.

traps.incorrect: The scientist which spoke won an award.
traps.correct: The scientist who spoke won an award.
traps.explanation: Use who for people.

traps.incorrect: The report, that was published yesterday, is useful.
traps.correct: The report, which was published yesterday, is useful.
traps.explanation: Non-defining relatives use which rather than that.

traps.incorrect: The professor whose published the study retired.
traps.correct: The professor who published the study retired.
traps.explanation: Whose needs a following noun phrase.

traps.incorrect: The data which collected yesterday were reliable.
traps.correct: The data collected yesterday were reliable.
traps.explanation: Passive reduced relative uses past participle.

traps.incorrect: This is the method which we rely.
traps.correct: This is the method on which we rely.
traps.explanation: Rely needs on; alternatively the method which we rely on.

traps.incorrect: The paper makes clear about the problem.
traps.correct: The paper makes the problem clear.
traps.explanation: Make clear takes a direct object or a that-clause.

traps.incorrect: He described about the graph.
traps.correct: He described the graph.
traps.explanation: Describe is transitive without about.

traps.incorrect: The explanation is briefly and clear.
traps.correct: The explanation is brief and clear.
traps.explanation: Parallel predicate adjectives should be adjective forms.
